section_summary: This section covers late July through August 1940, focusing on the downfall of the moderate Yonai Cabinet and the establishment of the second government of Prince Fumimaro Konoe. Detailed diplomatic reports analyze Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka's pro-Axis foreign policy, the official proclamation of the 'Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere', and Konoe's movement to construct a 'New National Structure' transcending Western party politics while remaining distinct from European single-party fascism. Accompanying State Department memoranda and journalistic appraisals from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew, political adviser Stanley K. Hornbeck, and correspondent A. T. Steele evaluate Japan's continued economic dependence on the United States and the British Empire, emphasizing the deterrent capability of the U.S. Pacific Fleet stationed at Hawaii.

subfiles.about: Reports the foreign policy tenets formulated by incoming Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka and the revival of cabinet liaison conferences.
subfiles.summary: This concluding section of telegram 603 reports that the Foreign Office views world affairs as undergoing a transitional era marked by the decline of Britain and France and the rise of Germany, Italy, and the Soviet Union. To meet this transition, Foreign Minister Matsuoka's policy will center on strengthening ties with the Axis, establishing East Asiatic independence, and settling the China Incident and relations with the United States. Grew warns that while Japan desires an equitable settlement in the Pacific, continued confrontation backed by U.S. naval power could lead to war as the only logical outcome. A conference of the four principal ministers opened that afternoon.
subfiles.title: Telegram 603 (Section Two) from Tokyo regarding Japanese Foreign Policy under Matsuoka

subfiles.about: Reports press accounts of Yoshisuke Ayukawa's sudden arrival in Tokyo from Hsinking to present crucial economic and foreign policy recommendations to the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits a translated summary of an article from the Yomiuri Shimbun concerning Yoshisuke Ayukawa, President of the Manchurian Industrial Corporation, who unexpectedly flew from Hsinking to Tokyo. Ayukawa's mission involves presenting high-level recommendations on economic and international policies to the newly forming Konoe Cabinet. The proposal was coordinated in advance with incoming Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka and discussed with Lieutenant General Hideki Tojo during their flight to the capital. The article indicates that adopting Ayukawa's recommendations will produce at least a superficial alteration in Japanese foreign policy.
subfiles.title: Telegram 599 from Tokyo regarding Yoshisuke Ayukawa's Recommendations to the New Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reports the arrival in Manila of Japanese Diet members and the travel of Admiral Kichisaburo Nomura aboard the Saipan Maru bound for Davao and the South Seas.
subfiles.summary: High Commissioner Sayre reports that five members and two secretaries of the Japanese House of Representatives visited Manila, called on American and Philippine officials, and were entertained at luncheon by President Manuel Quezon. The delegation departed Manila for Davao to board the Saipan Maru for a tour of North Borneo, Celebes, and the Japanese mandated islands. The Japanese Consulate General additionally reported that Admiral Kichisaburo Nomura is traveling on the same vessel for health reasons, prompting requests to Philippine Commonwealth authorities for special police protection.
subfiles.title: Telegram 471 from Manila regarding Japanese Diet Members and Admiral Nomura Visiting the Philippines

subfiles.about: Reports Premier-designate Konoe's consultations with the Emperor and military leaders, and the initial selection of core cabinet ministers.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Premier-designate Prince Fumimaro Konoe had an extended audience with the Emperor and conferred with former service ministers to establish basic policies prior to selecting the full cabinet. Key issues slated for a four-minister conference include reconsidering non-involvement in the European war and strengthening the Rome-Berlin-Tokyo Axis. The Tokyo press, led by the Nichi Nichi, strongly endorsed intimate army-cabinet collaboration to unite supreme command with civil administration. Key ministers chosen include Lieutenant General Hideki Tojo (War), Vice Admiral Zengo Yoshida (Navy), and Yosuke Matsuoka (Foreign Affairs).
subfiles.title: Telegram 595 from Tokyo regarding Formation of the Second Konoe Cabinet and Ministerial Selections

subfiles.about: Reports Yoshisuke Ayukawa's extended conference with Prince Konoe regarding foreign loans and economic expansion for the Manchuria Industrial Development Company.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that Yoshisuke Ayukawa conferred with Prince Konoe for over ninety minutes, presenting vital recommendations on economic affairs closely tied to the incoming cabinet's diplomatic agenda. In an interview published in Yomiuri, Ayukawa explained that he briefed Konoe on obtaining foreign loans for the Manchuria Industrial Development Company, an initiative dating back to the first Konoe administration. Noting Japan's limited capital and natural resources, Ayukawa urged the government to seize economic opportunities arising from international developments, observing that the United States is not the only nation capable of providing credit.
subfiles.title: Telegram 605 from Tokyo regarding Ayukawa's Conference with Prince Konoe on Foreign Loans

subfiles.about: Transmits the official roster of ministers selected for the newly formed second cabinet of Prince Fumimaro Konoe.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that Prince Konoe has finalized his cabinet slate, awaiting only the arrival of two members in Tokyo for formal investiture. The roster comprises Yosuke Matsuoka (Foreign Affairs), Eiji Yasui (Home and Welfare), Isao Kawata (Finance), Hideki Tojo (War), Zengo Yoshida (Marine), Akira Kazami (Justice), Kunihiko Hashida (Education), Tadaatsu Ishiguro (Agriculture and Forestry), Ichizo Kobayashi (Commerce and Industry), Shozo Murata (Communications and Railways), and Naoki Hoshino (Minister Without Portfolio and Director General of Cabinet Planning Board).
subfiles.title: Telegram 608 from Tokyo Announcing the Slate of the Second Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reports Wilfrid Fleisher's confidential background interview with incoming Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka regarding totalitarianism and foreign relations.
subfiles.summary: Grew summarizes an impromptu, off-the-record interview given by Yosuke Matsuoka to Wilfrid Fleisher of the Japan Advertiser and New York Herald Tribune prior to taking office. Matsuoka asserted that democracy is bankrupt, that totalitarianism will inevitably achieve worldwide supremacy, and that credits or loans cannot bridge differences between incompatible political and economic systems. He advocated a domestic single-party structure rooted in popular devotion to the Emperor rather than European-style coercion. Fleisher concluded that Matsuoka displayed an intense pro-Axis bias exceeding that of any other Japanese official he had encountered.
subfiles.title: Telegram 606 from Tokyo regarding Wilfrid Fleisher's Interview with Yosuke Matsuoka

subfiles.about: Provides a confidential State Department departmental summary of Tokyo telegram 606 regarding Fleisher's conversation with Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: This confidential State Department summary condenses Ambassador Grew's report of Wilfrid Fleisher's background interview with Foreign Minister Matsuoka. The text highlights Matsuoka's declarations that democracy is doomed, that totalitarianism will endure for centuries, and that American talk of economic aid to Japan is a fallacy. It reviews Matsuoka's long advocacy of a single national structure based on imperial loyalty, as well as Fleisher's observation of Matsuoka's profound pro-Axis sympathies, while noting that his practical policy toward the United States remains to be determined.
subfiles.title: State Department Summary of Telegram 606 regarding Fleisher's Interview with Matsuoka

subfiles.about: Confirms the formal investiture of the second Konoe Cabinet and Matsuoka's concurrent portfolio as Minister for Overseas Affairs.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew briefly confirms that the new cabinet headed by Prince Fumimaro Konoe was formally invested by the Emperor on the night of July 22, 1940. The ministerial composition conforms to the lineup previously communicated in telegram 608. In addition to his appointment as Minister for Foreign Affairs, Yosuke Matsuoka assumed the portfolio of Minister for Overseas Affairs concurrently.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Tokyo Reporting the Formal Investiture of the Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reports Premier Konoe's first press interview and his initial nationwide radio address denouncing liberal party politics.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that Premier Konoe gave his first press conference following the cabinet's formation, adopting nebulous language to avoid specific commitments regarding future policies. In a radio address delivered to the nation that evening, Konoe condemned traditional political parties, asserting that concepts rooted in liberalism, democracy, and socialism are fundamentally incompatible with Japan's national polity. Konoe insisted on an urgent reorganization of the domestic economy to eradicate Japan's economic reliance on foreign powers.
subfiles.title: Telegram 614 from Tokyo on Premier Konoe's First Press Interview and Radio Address

subfiles.about: Argues that maintaining the U.S. Battle Fleet in the Pacific and at Hawaii is essential to back potential trade embargoes and deter Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Political adviser Stanley K. Hornbeck calls Under Secretary Welles's attention to paragraph four of Grew's telegram 613, agreeing that economic considerations constrain immediate radical shifts in Japanese foreign policy. Hornbeck emphasizes that the threat of U.S. import and export embargoes exercises a powerful restraining influence on Japanese leaders only so long as the U.S. Battle Fleet remains positioned in the Pacific at Hawaii. If the fleet were redeployed to the Atlantic, Japanese fears of embargoes would evaporate, whereas its Pacific deployment maintains a critical political equilibrium in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Under Secretary Sumner Welles regarding U.S. Embargoes and Fleet Deterrence

subfiles.about: Provides a detailed political analysis of the collapse of the Yonai Cabinet, Konoe's return to power, and the factors governing Japanese foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew analyzes the transition from the Yonai administration to the second Konoe Cabinet, attributing the shift to popular frustration over the protracted China war and a desire to capitalize on European Axis victories. He evaluates the new cabinet as predominantly conservative, with nationalist planners like Naoki Hoshino and Akira Kazami pushing for an economic bloc and electoral reform. Grew assesses that Japan is unlikely to make an abrupt break toward the Axis in the immediate future because of its heavy economic dependence on the United States and the British Empire for vital raw materials and export markets.
subfiles.title: Telegram 613 from Tokyo Assessing the Fall of the Yonai Cabinet and Outlook under Konoe

subfiles.about: Synthesizes Ambassador Grew's political appraisal in telegram 613 regarding the Yonai Cabinet's fall and Konoe's diplomatic constraints.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum provides a structured summary of Ambassador Grew's telegram 613. It outlines the economic factors preventing an immediate, definitive Japanese commitment to the Axis powers, given Japan's inability to obtain raw materials or market manufactures within the Axis bloc. The memo reviews Admiral Yonai's skepticism toward Germany and Italy, the domestic political pressures that unseated him, popular hopes for concluding the China conflict under Konoe, and the cabinet's ideological makeup.
subfiles.title: State Department Far Eastern Division Summary of Telegram 613

subfiles.about: Reports the resignation of Masayuki Tani as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew informs the Department of State of announcements in the Tokyo vernacular press reporting the resignation of Masayuki Tani from his post as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs following the formation of the new Konoe administration.
subfiles.title: Telegram 617 from Tokyo Reporting the Resignation of Vice Foreign Minister Masayuki Tani

subfiles.about: Transmits Vice Consul Beppo R. Johansen's report of an overheard train conversation between two Japanese expressing severe distress over Japanese ventures in Manchuria and China.
subfiles.summary: Consul Merrell forwards a memorandum by Vice Consul Johansen detailing a candid conversation overheard on a passenger train between Peiping and Mukden between an educated scholar and a technical expert. The Japanese travelers expressed impassioned concern over their nation's future, asserting that developmental efforts in Manchukuo are crippled by incompetent personnel and premature economic policies. They questioned the utility of anti-British agitation, criticized state propaganda and the Diet uproar over Takao Saito, and warned that antagonizing Great Britain and the United States would lead Japan to ruin.
subfiles.title: Despatch 262 from Harbin Transmitting Vice Consul Johansen's Report of an Overheard Japanese Conversation

subfiles.about: Summarizes the official Japanese Government announcement setting forth fundamental national policies and the creation of a national defense state.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits an official summary provided by the Foreign Office outlining the Konoe Government's basic national policies. The declaration proclaims an urgent need for fundamental governmental renovations to build an advanced national defense state, prioritizing the creation of a new order in Greater East Asia rooted in the solidarity of Japan, Manchukuo, and China. Domestically, the program calls for administrative reform, educational renovation, a planned national defense economy, and a simplified standard of living to withstand prolonged national hardships.
subfiles.title: Telegram 640 from Tokyo on the Japanese Government's Fundamental National Policy Outline

subfiles.about: Transmits Foreign Minister Matsuoka's public declaration on proclaiming the Imperial Way ('kodo') and creating a Greater East Asian chain of common prosperity.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards the text of an official statement issued by Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka defining Japan's world mission as proclaiming and demonstrating the Imperial Way (kodo). Matsuoka defines this mission in international relations as enabling all nations and races to find their proper place in the world. The immediate diplomatic objective is to establish a great East Asian chain of common prosperity linked by Japan, Manchukuo, and China, while collaborating resolutely with friendly powers ready to cooperate with Japan.
subfiles.title: Telegram 642 from Tokyo Transmitting Statement by Foreign Minister Matsuoka on the 'Kodo' and Greater East Asia

subfiles.about: Reports the appointment of Chuichi Ohashi as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs succeeding Masayuki Tani.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports press announcements that Chuichi Ohashi, recently serving as Counselor to the Manchukuo Government, has been appointed Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs in succession to Masayuki Tani.
subfiles.title: Telegram 651 from Tokyo Reporting Chuichi Ohashi's Appointment as Vice Foreign Minister

subfiles.about: Surveys critical Tokyo press editorials regarding the vague and abstract nature of the Government's and Foreign Minister's policy pronouncements.
subfiles.summary: Grew summarizes editorial reactions from leading Tokyo newspapers regarding the policy declarations released by the Konoe Government and Foreign Minister Matsuoka. Press commentary was broadly critical, with Hochi dismissing the pronouncements as an abstract administrative wishlist lacking concrete execution plans, and Nichi Nichi regretting that the explanation of the 'new order' was too weak for international comprehension. In contrast, Yomiuri interpreted the statements as heralding a drastic departure from former Foreign Minister Arita's conciliatory approach in favor of a hardline diplomatic posture against opposing powers.
subfiles.title: Telegram 654 from Tokyo on Japanese Press Reactions to Government and Foreign Policy Statements

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo telegram 657 of August 3, 1940, filed under decimal classification 756D.94/57.
subfiles.summary: This official Department of State cross-reference sheet records that telegram 657 from Tokyo, dated August 3, 1940, has been classified and filed under subject decimal file 756D.94/57.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram 657 from Tokyo

subfiles.about: Reports Foreign Minister Matsuoka's press interview given on a train en route to Shinto shrines regarding Greater East Asia and ongoing diplomacy.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports on an informal press interview given by Foreign Minister Matsuoka aboard a train while traveling to national Shinto shrines to report his assumption of office. Matsuoka stressed two imperatives: accomplishing internal political reorganization and pursuing a 'positive diplomacy' to construct a sphere of mutual prosperity in Greater East Asia with likeminded friendly powers. He voiced optimism regarding Sino-Japanese negotiations between Nobuyuki Abe and Wang Ching-wei, adding that Japan will carefully observe the attitudes of Great Britain, the United States, Germany, Italy, and Russia before making further public declarations.
subfiles.title: Telegram 685 from Tokyo on Foreign Minister Matsuoka's Train Interview En Route to National Shrines

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo telegram 687 of August 12, 1940, filed under decimal classification 756D.94/58.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference sheet records that telegram 687 from Tokyo, dated August 12, 1940, has been transferred and filed under decimal classification 756D.94/58.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram 687 from Tokyo

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo telegram 693 of August 12, 1940, filed under decimal classification 756D.94/59.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference sheet indicates that telegram 693 from Tokyo, dated August 12, 1940, has been classified and filed under decimal classification 756D.94/59.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram 693 from Tokyo

subfiles.about: Reports confidential discussions with Foreign Minister Matsuoka at a dinner honoring Ambassador Steinhardt regarding domestic political reorganization and anti-foreign agitation.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports on an extensive private conversation with Foreign Minister Matsuoka during a dinner hosted for U.S. Ambassador to Moscow Laurence Steinhardt. Matsuoka explained that Konoe's impending announcement of the new national structure aims at eliminating all party politics and bickering rather than establishing a single political party. Expressing deep disgust at anti-foreign campaigns, Matsuoka revealed that he had unsuccessfully urged the Home Minister to ban an anti-British rally at Hibiya Hall and had severely reprimanded nationalist societies, warning that such agitation was unworthy of a civilized nation. Grew assesses Matsuoka's remarks as genuine and suggests he may be appealed to in dampening anti-American propaganda.
subfiles.title: Telegram 740 from Tokyo on Grew's Dinner Conversation with Foreign Minister Matsuoka

subfiles.about: Transmits excerpts of Premier Konoe's address to the opening session of the Preparatory Committee for the New National Structure.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits Foreign Office translation excerpts of Premier Konoe's address inaugurating the Preparatory Committee on the Establishment of the New National Structure. Konoe declared that concluding the China Affair and participating in the new world order requires building an advanced national defense state uniting horizontal and vertical segments of the populace. Crucially, Konoe rejected a Western-style single-party dictatorship as incompatible with Japan's fundamental constitutional principle of 'one sovereign over all', under which every subject possesses the direct duty and privilege of assisting the Imperial Throne.
subfiles.title: Telegram 759 from Tokyo Transmitting Excerpts of Premier Konoe's Address on the New National Structure

subfiles.about: Reports the appointments of Toshio Shiratori and Ryoei Saito as Diplomatic Advisers to the Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the Official Gazette's announcement of the appointments of Toshio Shiratori, former Ambassador to Italy, and Ryoei Saito as Diplomatic Advisers to the Foreign Office. The telegram outlines Saito's previous diplomatic and colonial career, including his service as Director of the Foreign Office Commercial Bureau, director of the South Manchuria Railway Company in 1927, and adviser to Kwantung Army Headquarters in 1929.
subfiles.title: Telegram 758 from Tokyo Reporting the Appointments of Toshio Shiratori and Ryoei Saito as Diplomatic Advisers

subfiles.about: Transmits the complete text in seven sections of Premier Konoe's opening address on the establishment of the New National Structure.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits the full seven-section official translation of Premier Konoe's address opening the Preparatory Committee for the New National Structure on August 28, 1940. Konoe detailed the permanent necessity of mobilizing total national energies across politics, economics, and culture to conclude the China Affair and create a new order in East Asia. He explained that while parliamentary party politics founded on liberalism are obsolete, a totalitarian single-party system where one party monopolizes the state is unacceptable under Japanese polity, which requires all subjects unitedly to obey Imperial decisions and assist the Throne.
subfiles.title: Telegram 760 from Tokyo Transmitting Full Text of Premier Konoe's Address on the New National Structure

subfiles.about: Transmits an analytical six-section report by Chicago Daily News correspondent A. T. Steele regarding political trends in Japan, German-Japanese relations, and American policy.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Robert L. Smyth transmits a detailed six-section report prepared by seasoned foreign correspondent A. T. Steele following his observations in Japan and Manchuria. Steele reports that Japan is rapidly embracing totalitarianism and pro-Axis opportunism in hopes of exploiting an early German victory over Britain, though Tokyo remains cautious due to Soviet Manchurian border vulnerabilities and China commitments. Steele notes that Germans view Japan opportunistically as a nuisance factor against the United States, and he strongly advises Washington that firmness and naval strength represent the safest American policy, as Japan is anxious to avoid a conflict with the United States unless forced as a last resort.
subfiles.title: Telegram 300 from Peiping Transmitting A. T. Steele's Observations on Japan, Axis Alignment, and U.S. Policy
